summary: This unit teaches you to communicate well as a team leader in a welding and fabrication workplace. You will learn to choose the right way to pass on a message, listen and question to get the facts, give clear instructions and briefings, run toolbox talks and meetings, read and write workplace documents, use the phone and two-way radio correctly, deal with clients, give and receive feedback, and handle conflict calmly and fairly.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 2 you followed instructions and passed on simple messages. At Level 3 you **lead the communication**: you brief a team, run short meetings, take and follow up client calls, read and explain technical documents, write notes and reports, and sort out problems between people.

Poor communication causes more wasted steel, rework and accidents than poor welding. A cut list read wrongly, a change agreed by phone but never written down, a crane signal misunderstood, a hazard reported but not passed on: each starts with a message that did not get through. Good communication is a safety skill and a quality skill.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders and fabricators who lead a team, deal with clients or work alongside other trades.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Choose how to communicate
Decide whether a message is best spoken, written, shown, or all three, and who needs to receive it.
Listen and question
Listen actively, ask open and closed questions to get the facts, and check that people have understood.
Overcome barriers
Deal with noise, PPE, distance, trade terms, language and people's feelings, so the message gets through.
Give instructions and briefings
Explain a job's aim, steps, roles, hazards and checks; show how; lead toolbox talks; use signs and signals correctly.
Take part in and lead meetings
Plan an agenda, chair fairly, record decisions and actions, follow them up, and consult the team before changes.
Read and write at work
Read drawings, job cards, the WPS and safety data sheets; write clear handover notes, emails, messages and short reports.
Use the phone and radio, and deal with clients
Take and pass on messages accurately, use radio procedure, handle complaints and changes politely, and keep information confidential.
Give feedback and handle conflict
Give and receive feedback about the work, settle disagreements by the facts, raise problems through the right channel, and review how well the team communicated.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on choosing how to communicate, listening and questioning, barriers, instructions, meetings, documents, writing, phone and radio, clients, feedback and conflict.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as feedback, chain of command, closed question, RFI and BCC) and essays on how you would brief a team, run a meeting, handle a conflict or deal with a client.
Two **group practicals**: planning and leading a job briefing and a toolbox talk; and handling a client complaint through a phone call, a team meeting and written follow-up, using role play.

blocks.note: In the practicals, the assessor listens to how you speak (plain words, a steady pace, facing the group), whether you ask open questions to check understanding, and whether actions are written down with names and dates.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Every message has a **sender**, the **message** itself, a **channel** (speech, a radio, a note, a drawing, a hand signal), and a **receiver**. The message is only complete when the receiver understands it and the sender knows that he or she has. The reply or reaction that shows this is **feedback**.

flow: The sender decides what the receiver needs to know and do
The sender chooses the words, pictures or signals
The message travels by a channel: face to face, phone, radio, paper, screen, sign
The receiver hears or reads it and works out what it means
The receiver gives feedback: an answer, a read-back, an action, a question
The sender checks the feedback and corrects any misunderstanding

blocks.p: Anything that spoils the message on the way is a **barrier**: grinding noise, a mumbled word, a trade term the receiver does not know, a smudged note, or a receiver who is tired or angry.

head: Method
Best for
Weaknesses
Examples
rows: Spoken (face to face, phone, radio)
Quick messages, briefings, questions, emergencies: you get feedback at once
People forget or mishear; no record
Start-of-shift briefing, a quick question to the fitter, a radio call to the crane
Written (paper or screen)
Sizes, settings, changes, agreements, anything that must be checked later
Slower; can be misread if unclear; no chance to ask at once
Job card, cut list, handover note, email to a client, report, minutes
Visual (drawings, signs, signals, sketches, photos)
Shapes and sizes, places where speech fails, people who read little
Must be understood the same way by everyone; signals must be agreed first
Drawing, safety sign, crane hand signal, marked-up photo, HOT written on steel

blocks.note: For anything important, use **more than one** method: say it, show it and write it. A change to a job is explained at the briefing, marked on the drawing and recorded in the job file, so that both shifts work from the same information.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Formal** communication goes through set channels and is usually recorded: job cards, drawings, permits, reports, minutes, emails to clients.

**Informal** communication is everyday talk: a word at the bench, a chat at lunch. It builds trust and passes on quick information, but it is not a reliable way to pass on a change, a hazard or an agreement.
Rumours (the 'grapevine') spread fast and are often wrong. Put out clear facts early, before a rumour fills the gap.

blocks.p: Every workplace has a **chain of command**: the line of reporting from worker to team leader, supervisor and manager. It makes sure problems reach the person who can act on them, and that instructions come from the person with the authority to give them.

ul: Raise a problem with your team leader or supervisor first, unless it is an emergency or the rules say otherwise.
If you are the team leader, pass messages both ways: from management to the team, and from the team back up.
Communicate sideways too: with the stores, the drawing office, other trades on site and the quality inspector.
Never let the chain of command stop a safety warning. Anyone may warn of danger at once, and anyone may stop a crane lift.

blocks.p: Before you pass on a message, ask: who must **act** on it, who must **know** about it, and who must **approve** it? A change to a gate design, for example, must reach the welders (act), the stores and the painter (know), and the supervisor and the client (approve).
Listening is the half of communication most people forget. **Active listening** means giving the speaker your full attention and showing that you have understood.

ul: Stop what you are doing, face the speaker, and look at them. Put the phone away.
Let the person finish. Do not interrupt or plan your answer while they talk.
Nod or say short words ('I see', 'go on') to show you are following.
Take notes when there are figures, names or dates.
Ask questions about anything unclear, including words you do not know.
Sum up what you heard in your own words ('So the electrodes spatter and stick, only on the new batch?') and let the speaker correct you.

head: Type
What it does
Example
rows: Open question
Gets the person to explain; cannot be answered with yes or no
'What happens when you strike the arc?' 'How will you set up this joint?'
Closed question
Gets a yes or no, or one fact; good for confirming
'Is the gas turned off at the cylinder?' 'What size is the root gap?'
Probing (follow-up) question
Digs deeper into an answer
'When did it start?' 'Is it the same on every machine?'
Clarifying question
Checks you have understood
'Do you mean the left-hand post, as you face the gate?'
Leading question (avoid)
Pushes the person towards the answer you want
'You checked the sling, didn't you?'

blocks.p: Use **open** questions to find out what someone knows or what happened. Use **closed** questions to confirm a single, exact fact, such as whether a sling's safe working load is more than the load.
'Do you understand?' nearly always gets a 'yes', from politeness, shyness or pride. It tells you nothing. Instead, ask the person to **tell you back** or **show you** what they will do.

ul: 'Tell me how you will set up this joint.'
'Which size matters most on this bracket, and how will you check it?'
'Show me where you will clamp the work.'
For figures and times on the phone or radio, **read them back**: 'That's 7:30 tomorrow, at the Linstead site, correct?'
Check the first piece of work early, so a misunderstanding is caught before it spreads.

blocks.p: If an engineer, client or supplier uses a word you do not know, ask what it means, and write it down. It is far better to ask once than to guess and cut the steel wrong. As a team leader, make it normal for your team to do the same.

**Non-verbal** communication is everything except the words: body language, facial expression, gestures, eye contact and tone of voice. People believe the tone and the body language more than the words.

ul: When you brief a team, face the group, stand where all can see you, make eye contact, and speak at a steady pace.
Folded arms, a raised voice or looking at your phone tell people you are not interested, whatever you say.
Watch the listeners too: blank looks, glancing at a phone or nodding without speaking may mean the message has not landed. Pause and ask them to explain it back.
Helmets, masks and ear defenders hide faces and muffle speech. Get the person's attention first, use agreed hand signals, or move somewhere you can take PPE off safely.

sections.title: Barriers to communication and respect for others

head: Barrier
Example in the shop
How to overcome it
rows: Noise
Grinders, hammering and machines drown out speech
Move to a quiet spot, or pause the noisy work; use agreed hand signals; put it in writing too
PPE
Ear defenders muffle words; helmets hide faces
Get attention first; lift PPE only where it is safe; use signals and written notes
Distance
The crane operator is 30 m away; the team is spread across a site
Radios used with proper procedure; one signaller in view
Trade terms and jargon
A new trainee does not know 'root face', 'land' or 'hi-lo'
Plain words; explain each term the first time; show the real thing
Language and reading
A worker reads little, or thinks in Patois; a client speaks only Spanish
Show and demonstrate; pictures and sketches; read documents aloud discreetly; find an interpreter for a visitor
Feelings and attitude
A worker is angry, worried, tired or shy; someone 'knows it all'
Choose a good time; stay calm; listen first; make it safe to ask questions
Passing it along
A message goes from manager to foreman to welder and changes on the way
Give important messages directly, and in writing
Unclear or too much information
A long, rambling briefing with ten points
Plan the message; keep to the few points that matter; one topic at a time
Poor timing or place
A briefing at 4:55 p.m. as people pack up
Brief at the start of the job, in a suitable place, with enough time

blocks.note: Most Jamaicans speak Jamaican Creole (Patois) every day, and many think in it. Drawings, procedures, permits and reports are written in Standard English. On the shop floor, use whichever language gets the message across, but write records in Standard English, and check that everyone has understood. Never mock the way someone speaks or reads: it stops people asking the questions that keep them safe.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A fabrication team may include people of different ages, sexes, faiths, parishes, backgrounds and abilities. Good communication treats everyone with respect, and it is also the law in many workplaces that people are not harassed or treated unfairly.

ul: Use people's names, not nicknames they do not like.
No jokes, remarks or 'banter' about a person's sex, colour, religion, body, disability, accent or where they come from. Something said 'just for a joke' can drive a good worker out.
Give everyone the same chance to speak and to be heard in briefings and meetings.
Respect different ways of working and different experience: the older welder's knowledge and the young trainee's questions both help the job.
If someone is mocked or harassed, a team leader deals with it promptly, privately and firmly, and reports it if it continues.

sections.title: Leading the team: instructions, briefings and demonstrations

flow: Prepare: read the job card, the drawing and the WPS yourself; know the aim, the steps, the hazards and the checks
Get the team together in a quiet place, with the drawing or the real part in front of you
Start with the aim of the job and each person's part in it
Go through the steps in order, in plain words, showing the drawing or the part
Point out the hazards and their controls, and the PPE
Say what will be checked, by whom and when (for example the diagonals before full welding)
Check understanding: ask each person to tell you their first step and the key size or check
Write the key points on the job card or a board, and check the first piece of work early

blocks.p: A good written instruction is short and exact: 'Grind a 30° bevel, leaving a 2 mm root face' is better than 'Prepare the edges properly'. Give sizes, units, quantities and the order of work.
For a practical skill, such as setting up an oxy-acetylene cutting torch or reading a micrometer, use four steps:

flow: **Explain:** what the task is, why it matters, the hazards
**Demonstrate:** do it slowly, step by step, explaining as you go
**Let them try:** each person does it while you watch and correct
**Check:** they do it on their own; you confirm they can, and record it

blocks.p: A **toolbox talk** is a short safety talk, usually 5 to 15 minutes, given at the work area before work starts.

ul: Keep to **one topic** linked to the day's work, such as grinding disc safety or working in the heat.
Plan three or four key points; bring a real item to show (a damaged disc, a frayed sling).
Stand where everyone can see and hear, away from noise; speak plainly; keep it short.
Ask questions ('What would you check before fitting a disc?') and let people share their own near misses.
Sum up the key points, record attendance on a sign-off sheet, and note any problems raised so they are fixed.

blocks.p: Confirm each person's task aloud in front of the whole group, so that no task is missed or done twice, and everyone knows who is doing what. Mention any changes since yesterday, any hazards on site today, and who to go to with problems.

head: Sign
Shape and colour
Meaning
rows: Prohibition
Red circle with a red diagonal bar, black symbol
You must not do this (no smoking, no naked flames)
Mandatory
Blue circle, white symbol
You must do this (wear eye protection, wear a welding helmet)
Warning
Yellow triangle with a black border and symbol
Danger: take care (electricity, hot surface, overhead load)
Safe condition
Green square or rectangle, white symbol
The way to safety (exit, first aid, eyewash)
Fire equipment
Red square or rectangle, white symbol
Where the fire equipment is (extinguisher, fire alarm point)

ul: Hot steel looks exactly like cold steel. Write **HOT** on it with soapstone or chalk, and tell the people nearby.
Barriers and tape mark an area people must not enter; take them down when the danger has gone, or people learn to ignore them.
A lock and a 'Do not operate' tag on an isolator mean exactly that: only the person who fitted them removes them.
Use the standard hand signals your site uses, and agree them with the operator before the lift.
Only **one named signaller** gives signals during a lift, so the operator never gets two signals that disagree. The signaller should be easy to pick out, for example by a coloured vest or armband.
If the operator cannot see the signaller, use a two-way radio on a channel kept for the lift.
**Anyone** who sees danger may give the emergency stop signal, and the operator must always obey it.
If the operator loses sight of the signaller, or a signal is not clear, the lift stops.
Decide the **purpose**: what must the meeting decide or share?
Invite only the people who need to be there, and set a finish time (production meetings are often 15 to 20 minutes).
Send out a short **agenda** beforehand: the items in order, with time for each.
Make the first item a **review of last meeting's actions**, so decisions are carried out.

head: Role
What they do
rows: Chair
Opens with the purpose and the finish time, takes each item in turn, lets each person speak, keeps people to the point, stops side arguments, sums up each decision
Minute-taker
Writes down the decisions and the actions: what, who and by when
Members
Come prepared, speak in turn, listen, keep to the item, accept the actions given to them

ul: If two people talk over each other, ask each to speak in turn, then sum up both views before moving on.

If an argument starts that is not on the agenda, or involves only two people, note it and agree a separate time to deal with it with the people involved ('parking' it), so the meeting can finish its business.
Bring quiet members in by name: 'Shanice, you work on that machine; what do you think?'
Keep to time. If an item needs more information, give someone the action to find it and bring it back.

blocks.p: A meeting is only useful if what it decided is done. End each item with an action, each with a **name** and a **date**, and read the action list back at the end so everyone agrees.

head: Action
Who
By when
rows: Repair the fume extractor in bay 2
Maintenance fitter
Wednesday
Order 50 cutting discs (125 mm)
Storeman
Tuesday
Brief both shifts on the new cut list for job 3311
Team leaders
Monday, start of shift

blocks.p: Send out or post the minutes within a day, and start the next meeting by checking each action.

blocks.h: Consulting the team before a change

blocks.p: Before changing how work is done (a new layout, a new form, new working hours), a good team leader asks the people who do the work. They often know problems the leader cannot see, such as a machine that is hard to reach. Being asked also helps them accept the change, and workers must be able to raise hazards that a change may bring.

flow: Explain the problem and the reason for the change
Ask for views at a team meeting, and give people a chance to speak privately or in writing too
Listen, note the ideas and the concerns, and answer them honestly
Decide, then explain what was decided and why, including why some ideas were not used
Review the change after a few weeks, and adjust it

head: Document
What it tells you
What to check
rows: Job card or work order
The job, the quantity, the due date, who it is for
Job number, quantity, date, special instructions
Drawing
Shapes, sizes, tolerances, weld symbols, material
The **revision** (Rev C is newer than Rev B); the title block; the units; the notes
Welding procedure specification (WPS)
The approved process, filler, settings, joint preparation and positions for a weld
That it is the right WPS for the joint, and that you can follow it
Safety data sheet (SDS)
The hazards of a chemical and how to use, store and dispose of it safely
The sections you need (see below)
Safe work procedure
The steps of a task in order, with the hazards and controls
Follow the steps in order; numbered steps let you find your place
Permit (hot work, confined space)
What is allowed, where, when and with which precautions
That it is signed, in date, and covers this exact job
Non-conformance report (NCR)
Work or material that does not meet the specification, and what will be done
The items affected and the decision on them
Request for information (RFI)
A written question to the engineer or designer, and the answer
That the answer is recorded before work goes on

blocks.p: If a written instruction can be read two ways, do not guess. Ask the person who wrote it what was meant, and note the answer on the document or in the job file. If you find a mistake (for example a size on the cut list that does not match the drawing), show it politely to the person responsible **before** any steel is cut.

blocks.h: Finding your way round a safety data sheet

blocks.p: A safety data sheet has 16 numbered sections in the same order for every product. Learn where the most-used ones are:

head: Section
Heading
Use it to find
rows: Hazards identification
What harm the product can do, with the warning pictograms
First-aid measures
What to do if it gets in the eyes or on the skin, or is swallowed or breathed in
Fire-fighting measures
Which extinguisher to use and any special dangers in a fire
Handling and storage
How to use and store it safely
Exposure controls and personal protection
Ventilation, and which gloves, eye protection and respirator to wear
Disposal considerations
How to get rid of the product and its containers

blocks.p: For the correct electrode current range, the right filler for a steel, or the drying time for a paint, go to the maker's data: the packet, the label or the data sheet.

ul: Put the main point first: what the reader needs to know or do.
Use short sentences and plain words. Give sizes, quantities, places, names and dates exactly.
Keep facts apart from opinions. 'The grinder guard was found off, on the bench' is a fact; 'someone was careless' is an opinion.
Write in Standard English, with correct trade terms, and read it through before you send it.
Write records such as incident reports as soon as possible, while the details are fresh.

blocks.h: A short report to the manager

blocks.p: When you report a problem on a job (a late delivery, a batch of rejected welds), keep it to a page and set it out under headings:

ul: Title, date, job number, and who it is to and from.

A **summary** of the main point in the first lines: what has happened, how it affects the job, and what you need. For example: '8 of the 20 brackets for job 3311 failed visual inspection today because of porosity; delivery will slip by one day unless we work Saturday.'
The facts in order: what was found, when, by whom and how it was checked.
The likely cause, and how it was found.
What has been done, and what is proposed, with names and dates.
Any decision or help needed from the manager, and the evidence attached (photos, the inspection sheet).

blocks.h: Charts and figures on the notice board

blocks.p: Shops post charts of reject rates, output and safety figures. Read the title, what each axis shows and the units before you draw a conclusion. A weld reject rate that falls from 12% to 4% over a month means fewer welds are failing inspection: the quality of the welding has improved. Ask what is being counted and over what period, so you explain the chart correctly to the team.
A **handover note** tells the next shift the state of the work. It is short, exact and organised by job or item.

ul: Date, shift and who wrote it.
For each item: what is done, what is not, and what to do next: 'Gate 2: hinges tacked only. Weld out and grind.'
Hazards and anything left isolated, locked off or on permit: 'Bay 3 extractor locked off for repair; do not weld in bay 3.'
Problems, changes and anything waiting: materials due, questions to the engineer.
Go through the note face to face with the next team leader when you can, so that he or she can ask questions.
A clear subject line: 'Job 3311: railing delivery now Thursday 12 November'.
To: the people who must act. CC (carbon copy): people who need to know. BCC (**blind carbon copy**): people whose addresses the others will not see, for example when one email goes to many clients.
To a client, be polite and specific: say sorry where it is due, give the reason, the new date and a contact.
Do not write in anger. If an email upsets you, wait, then reply to the facts.
When you send a photo of a defect to an engineer, add a note: the job, the joint, what the photo shows, and a scale in the picture.
Work photos and client details belong to the job, not to social media or private chat groups.

blocks.note: Never give out a client's personal details, prices or quotes to anyone else, whoever they say they are. Take a message instead and tell your supervisor. Jamaica's data protection law protects people's personal information, and quotes are confidential business information.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Answer promptly: greet the caller, give the business name and your name
Listen to the whole message without interrupting; take notes
Ask questions to get the facts: name, phone number, job number, what is needed
Read the key details back: names, numbers, dates and times
Promise only what you can do, with a real time: 'Mr Brown will call you back by 3 p.m. today'
Pass the message on at once, in writing, and check that the promise is kept

blocks.p: A phone message should say: who it is for; who called, from where, and their number; the date and time; the message; what was promised; and who took it.
If a supplier phones with a change, such as a delivery time, read it back, then send a short text or email to confirm it. That avoids a mix-up and leaves a record.

ul: Check you are on the right channel, and listen before you speak so you do not cut across someone.
Think first, then press the button, pause a moment, and speak clearly at a normal pace, with the radio a few centimetres from your mouth.
Say who you are calling, then who you are: 'Crane, this is Tamoy.'
Keep messages short; give numbers digit by digit if there is any doubt.
Release the button and wait for the reply. Never talk over a lift in progress.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Over
I have finished speaking and I am waiting for your reply
Out
I have finished, and no reply is needed (so 'over and out' makes no sense)
Say again
Please repeat your message: I did not hear it clearly
Received, or Roger
I have received your message and understood it
Stand by
Wait: I will come back to you
Stop, stop, stop
Stop the movement at once (used during lifts)

ul: Be polite and patient, even when the client is upset. Let them explain fully, show that you understand, and do not argue or blame other staff.
If you cannot answer a question, say so, find out, and call back at the time you promised.

If a client asks for a change after work has started, note exactly what they want, have it priced and its effect on the date worked out, and get it **confirmed in writing** before any work on it starts.
Keep the client informed: tell them early about a delay, with the reason and the new date. Bad news told early is better than bad news found out.
Record complaints, promises and agreements in the job file.
Give it soon after the work, and in private when it is a correction. Praise can be given in front of others.
Talk about the work, not the person: 'The weld failed the check' deals with the problem; 'You did a bad job' attacks the person.
Be specific: 'The fillet legs are 5 mm on the top plate and 8 mm on the bottom' is useful; 'Your welds are messy' is not.
Start with something that was done well; then say exactly what to change, and show how.
Agree the next step (for example two practice runs while you watch), and follow up to praise the improvement.
Listen without arguing or making excuses.
Ask questions to understand: which standard, which limit, what exactly to change.
Thank the person, act on it, and check later that the change worked.
Taking feedback well sets the example for your team.

blocks.p: Disagreements happen in every team: over equipment, overtime, who caused a fault, or how a job should be done. Left alone, they grow and slow the work. Deal with them early and fairly.

flow: Make sure the work is safe, and stop any shouting on the shop floor
Talk to each person in private; let each explain, and listen without taking sides
Find what each person really needs (for example, both need the same machine in the morning)
Bring them together; keep to the facts and the job, not personal remarks
Ask them for solutions, and agree one (a booking time, a change in the order of work)
Write down what was agreed, tell others it affects, and check a few days later that it is working
If it continues, report it to your supervisor

ul: Raise a problem as soon as you find it, with the person who can fix it, and through the chain of command.
Bring the facts: what, where, when, and any evidence (a photo, a reading).
Thank people who report problems to you, act on what they say, and tell them what was done, or they will stop reporting.
If a hazard is reported (for example a fume extractor not working), stop the work it affects if needed, and report it at once.

blocks.p: After a job, hold a short review with the team: what went well, what went wrong, and what to change next time. Ask specific questions ('Did everyone know about the drawing change in time?'), note the answers, and use them on the next job.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can describe the communication process and explain why feedback completes it.
I can choose spoken, written or visual communication to suit a message, and use more than one for important messages.
I can explain the chain of command and work through it, without letting it delay a safety warning.
I can listen actively and sum up what I heard.
I can use open, closed, probing and clarifying questions, and avoid leading ones.
I can check understanding by asking people to tell me back or show me, and read back figures.
I can name the barriers to communication in a fabrication shop and overcome each one.
I can communicate respectfully with people of every background, and deal with disrespect.
I can give clear instructions and a job briefing, and show someone how to do a task.
I can plan and lead a toolbox talk.
I can read safety signs and use crane signals and warnings correctly.
I can plan, chair and minute a short meeting, and follow up its actions.
I can consult my team before a change.
I can find what I need in a drawing, a WPS, a job card and a safety data sheet.
I can write clear handover notes, messages, emails and short reports, keeping facts apart from opinions.
I can take and pass on phone messages, and use two-way radio procedure.
I can deal politely with clients' questions, complaints and changes, and keep information confidential.
I can give and receive feedback, handle conflict fairly, and raise problems through the right channel.

terms: Active listening
Giving the speaker full attention and showing you have understood, for example by summing up
Agenda
The list of items to be dealt with at a meeting, in order
Barrier
Anything that stops a message being received clearly
BCC
Blind carbon copy: an email copy whose address the other receivers cannot see
Chain of command
The line of reporting at work, from worker to supervisor to manager
Chair
The person who runs a meeting
Closed question
A question that can be answered with yes, no or a single fact
Feedback
The reply or reaction that shows the sender whether a message was understood
Handover note
A short written note for the next shift about the state of the work
Minutes
The written record of a meeting's decisions and actions
Non-verbal communication
Body language, facial expression, gestures and tone, without words
NCR
Non-conformance report: a record of work or material that does not meet the specification
Open question
A question that needs an explanation, not just yes or no
Over
Radio word: I have finished and am waiting for your reply
Read-back
Repeating figures, names or times back to the sender to confirm them
Revision (Rev)
A numbered or lettered change to a drawing or document
RFI
Request for information: a written question to the engineer or designer
SDS
Safety data sheet: the 16-section sheet on a chemical's hazards and safe use
Toolbox talk
A short safety talk at the work area before work starts
WPS
Welding procedure specification: the approved method for a weld

c1.title: Shift handover at a tank yard in Hayes
c1.text: Fitzroy leads the day shift at a yard in Hayes, Clarendon, that builds large steel water tanks. At 6 p.m. he hands over to Odane, who leads the night shift. Tank 3's roof plates are tacked but not welded. The crane's left outrigger pad is cracked and must not be used. The client has asked for a manway on Tank 4 to be moved 300 mm to the left: Fitzroy agreed on the phone, but nothing is in writing yet. Odane's crew has a copy of the Tank 4 drawing at Rev D; the office copy is Rev E.

c2.title: Setting a tank stand at a school in Port Maria
c2.text: Tamoy is the team leader fitting a 3 m high steel tank stand at a primary school in Port Maria, St Mary. A hired mobile crane will lift the stand from the truck onto its footings. A generator is running, the team are wearing ear defenders, and children are playing in the yard nearby. The team has two-way radios, and the crane operator, Mr Chin, cannot see the footings from his cab.

c3.title: A phone enquiry in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: Nadine works in the office of a fabrication shop in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. Mrs Ellis phones, upset and talking fast, to ask why her quote for burglar bars is higher than her neighbour's. Nadine does not know how the quote was worked out; the estimator, Garfield, is out until 2 p.m. Later the same day, a man phones saying he is Mrs Ellis's son and asks for her home address and the amount of her deposit.

c4.title: A new trainee in Browns Town
c4.text: Jhenelle has just joined a steel shop in Browns Town, St Ann, as a trainee. She is the only woman in the team. She reads well but does not yet know the shop's trade terms. When she asks what a 'root face' is, a senior welder, Clive, laughs and says, 'Every pickney know that.' In briefings she rarely speaks. The team leader is Marlon.

c5.title: The Monday meeting in Linstead
c5.text: Every Monday at 7:30 a.m. the team leaders at a fabrication shop in Linstead, St Catherine, meet for 20 minutes. Last week the meeting ran for an hour, half of it an argument about overtime, and nothing was written down. Two actions from the week before, repairing the extractor in bay 2 and ordering cutting discs, were never done. This week Shanique will chair. The manager also plans to move job cards onto tablets, and asks Shanique to find out what the welders think.

questions.q: Fitzroy has written a clear handover note. Why should he also go through it face to face with Odane?
o: So that Odane can ask questions and Fitzroy can check he understood
Because a handover note on its own has no real value as a record of work
So that Odane does not have to read the note during his shift
Because night-shift leaders are not allowed to sign written notes
questions.why: Writing gives a record; speaking gives instant feedback. Using both means Odane can ask about anything unclear, such as the cracked outrigger pad, and Fitzroy can confirm the message got through.

questions.q: What should happen about the manway change before the night shift works on Tank 4?
o: Odane cuts it 300 mm to the left, as Fitzroy agreed by phone
Odane phones the client tonight and decides with her himself
Work waits for written confirmation and a revised drawing
Odane cuts it where the drawing shows it, to be on the safe side
questions.why: A change agreed only by phone can be misremembered or disputed, and steel cut in the wrong place is costly to put right. It must be confirmed in writing and shown on a revised drawing before anyone cuts.

questions.q: Odane's crew has the Tank 4 drawing at Rev D, and the office has Rev E. What should the crew do?
o: Work from Rev D, since it is the copy the crew was actually given
Work from Rev E once confirmed as current, and mark Rev D superseded
Use whichever of the two is easier to read under the night-shift lights
Use Rev D for the sizes and Rev E for any of the welding details
questions.why: A later revision replaces the earlier one. The crew must work only from the current revision, and old copies are marked superseded or withdrawn so no one builds from them by mistake.

questions.q: Mr Chin cannot see the footings from his cab. How should the lift be directed?
o: Each team member signals to him whenever they see a problem
Tamoy shouts the directions to him from beside the footings
Mr Chin lowers the stand slowly and listens out for the team
One named signaller, by radio on a channel kept for the lift
questions.why: With a single signaller the operator never gets two instructions that disagree, and a radio on its own channel overcomes the distance and the noise when he cannot see the hand signals.

questions.q: On the radio, Mr Chin says something that Tamoy does not catch. What should she say?
o: 'Say again', and wait for him to repeat it
'Roger', then ask a team member what he meant
'Over and out', then switch to another channel
Nothing, and wave to him so that he carries on
questions.why: 'Say again' asks for the message to be repeated. 'Roger' would tell him she had understood when she had not, which is dangerous during a lift.

questions.q: The team's ear defenders and the generator make speech hard to hear. What is the best way for them to communicate during the lift?
o: Take off their ear defenders whenever someone speaks
Shout louder so they can be heard over the generator
Use hand signals agreed with everyone before the lift
Phone each other on their mobiles whenever they need to speak
questions.why: Agreed hand signals work where speech fails, provided everyone learns them before the lift starts. Removing hearing protection near a running generator, or phoning during a lift, brings new risks.

questions.q: What should Tamoy tell the school's principal before the lift?
o: The weight of the stand and the make and size of the crane
When the lift is, which area to keep clear, and a contact
Only that the team will be working on the premises that day
That the children may watch the lift from beside the truck
questions.why: The principal needs to know what to do: when, which area children and staff must keep out of, and a contact person. Technical details mean little to her, and nobody should stand near a load being lifted.

questions.q: Mrs Ellis is upset and talking fast. What should Nadine do first?
o: Explain at once that her neighbour's job was different
Let her finish, then sum up her concern back to her
Put the call through to the workshop straight away
Ask her to call back tomorrow when she is calmer
questions.why: Listening fully and summing up shows the caller she has been heard and checks that Nadine has the facts right. Interrupting with an explanation, or passing her on, usually makes an upset caller more upset.

questions.q: Nadine cannot explain the price herself. What is the best thing to promise Mrs Ellis?
o: 'Someone will get back to you as soon as possible.'
'I will look at the quote and lower the price for you.'
'Garfield will phone you back by 3 p.m. today.'
'Please call again later and ask for the estimator.'
questions.why: A specific person and a real time she can rely on shows respect and is easy to check. 'As soon as possible' is vague, and Nadine has no authority to change a price.

questions.q: Garfield emails Mrs Ellis to explain her quote. What should come first in the email?
o: A thank-you for her call and the answer to her question
The neighbour's quote, so she can compare the two prices
The shop's full price list for all its burglar-bar styles
The shop's terms and conditions for all quotes and deposits
questions.why: Put the main point first: the answer she asked for. The neighbour's quote is confidential and must never be shared, and price lists or terms can follow if they are needed.

questions.q: A man phones saying he is Mrs Ellis's son and asks for her address and the amount of her deposit. What should Nadine do?
o: Give him the details, since he says he is family
Give the address only, but not the deposit amount
Ask him to confirm her phone number, then give the details
Not give them, and offer to pass a message to Mrs Ellis
questions.why: Nadine cannot know who the caller really is, and a client's personal and payment details are confidential under the data protection law. Taking a message lets Mrs Ellis decide, and Nadine should tell her supervisor.

questions.q: What should Marlon do about Clive's remark?
o: Ignore it, since it was meant only as a joke
Tell Jhenelle that she will need to toughen up in a steel shop
Speak to Clive privately: remarks like that are not acceptable
Tell Clive off loudly, in front of the whole team, there and then
questions.why: Mocking someone for asking stops people asking the questions that keep them safe. A prompt, private and firm word sets the standard without a public scene; if it carries on, Marlon reports it.

questions.q: Marlon asks Jhenelle to explain 'root face' back to him, and she does so correctly, partly in Patois. What should he do?
o: Ask her to repeat it all in Standard English first
Explain it to her again using more technical words
Give her a written test on all the shop's terms
Accept it, and show her the term used on drawings
questions.why: The check is about understanding, and she has shown she understands. Spoken explanations can be in whatever language works; written records and drawings use the Standard English term, so he points her to it.

questions.q: Jhenelle rarely speaks in briefings. How can Marlon make it easier for her to raise questions?
o: Ask 'Any questions?' at the end of every single briefing
Ask open questions, and check with her privately after
Take her silence to mean that she has understood
Make her speak first at every team briefing from now on
questions.why: Shy or new people seldom answer 'Any questions?' in front of a group. Open questions, and a quiet word afterwards, give her a safe chance to ask, and show whether she has understood.

questions.q: What should Shanique send out before the meeting?
o: A short agenda with the items and the finish time
Last month's production figures for every job in full
A list of the people who came late to last week's meeting
Nothing, since everyone already knows what it is for
questions.why: An agenda lets people come prepared and keeps the meeting to its purpose and its time. Last week's meeting ran over because nothing set out what it had to cover.

questions.q: What should be the first item on this week's agenda?
o: The manager's plan to move job cards onto tablets
A vote to settle the overtime argument for good
Last week's actions: the extractor and the discs
A general discussion of any problems people have
questions.why: Starting with the actions from last time makes sure decisions are carried out. The broken extractor is also a safety matter that has been left for over a week.

questions.q: Halfway through, the overtime argument starts again between two leaders. As chair, what should Shanique do?
o: Let them argue it out, so it is settled once and for all
Note it, and agree a separate time with the two involved
End the meeting early and send everyone back to work
Take a quick vote of everyone present to decide it
questions.why: 'Parking' an off-agenda dispute keeps the meeting to its business and its time, while the people involved still get a proper chance to sort it out. A quick vote decides nothing about the real problem.

questions.q: How should Shanique find out what the welders think about job cards on tablets?
o: Send a memo giving the date the tablets will start
Ask only the two longest-serving welders for their views
Wait until the tablets arrive and see who complains
Explain why, ask everyone's views, and report back
questions.why: Consulting means explaining the reason, asking everyone (including those who will not speak up in a group), listening, and telling them what was decided and why. The people who use the job cards will spot problems the manager cannot.

questions.q: A new tin of zinc-rich primer arrives with its safety data sheet. Where on the sheet will you find what to do if it splashes in someone's eye?
o: The handling and storage section
The first-aid measures section
The exposure controls and personal protection section
The physical and chemical properties section
questions.why: First-aid measures (section 4 of a 16-section SDS) tell you what to do for eye or skin contact, swallowing or breathing it in. Read it before you use the product, not after an accident.

questions.q: What does a safety sign with a white symbol in a blue circle mean?
o: You must not do this, for example no naked flames
Danger: take care, for example a hot surface
You must do this, for example wear eye protection
The way to safety, for example the first-aid room
questions.why: Blue circles are mandatory signs. Prohibition signs are red circles with a bar, warning signs are yellow triangles, and safe-condition signs are green squares or rectangles.
